web_evidence.title: Excerpt from South of Broad by Pat Conroy
web_evidence.note: A three-page prologue excerpt, reproduced by permission of Nan A. Talese/Random House, sustains Leo's participating I/my narration through his family history and childhood.

web_evidence.title: Letter to Readers August 2009
web_evidence.note: On his official site, Conroy identifies Leo King as the narrator of South of Broad and describes presenting Charleston through Leo's eyes and following Leo's life.

web_evidence.title: The King of Charleston Writers
web_evidence.note: A contemporary author interview identifies Leo as both the novel's hero and narrator, and quotes Conroy discussing his construction of that narrator.

web_evidence.title: South of Broad Summary
web_evidence.note: The study guide identifies protagonist Leopold Bloom King as narrator and describes his narration across the novel's late-1960s and late-1980s periods.

web_evidence.title: The Prince of Tears
web_evidence.note: The full-book review treats the narrative as Leo's story and reproduces an interior passage in which Leo recounts finding his brother using first-person references.

person_note: The authorized prologue and numerous Goodreads event passages independently expose Leo King as a participating I-narrator. Conroy's own whole-book description identifies Leo as the narrator, while additional structural sources agree and reveal no alternating-person sections. Third-person references in several quotes describe Leo's father, mother, and friends from within that first-person account; dialogue, generic-you aphorisms, and clipped passages were not promoted to competing narrative persons. The main limitation is that the authorized sustained excerpt covers the opening, but the author-level structural evidence and widely distributed first-person event quotes resolve the whole book with high confidence.
